storms.name: Tropical cyclone (hurricane)

intro.q: A warm-core non-frontal synoptic-scale cyclone, originating over tropical or subtropical waters, with organized deep convection and a closed surface wind circulation about a well-defined center. Once formed, a tropical cyclone is maintained by the extraction of heat energy from the ocean at high temperature and heat export at the low temperatures of the upper troposphere.

conditions.q: Sea-surface temperatures of at least 26.5 degrees Celsius or 80 degrees Fahrenheit (usually).
A location (usually) at least five degrees of latitude (roughly 300 nautical miles) away from the equator.
Low values of vertical wind shear between roughly 5,000 and 38,000 feet (generally less than 10 meters per second, or 20 knots).

If the storm is far enough from the equator (generally at least 8 degrees of latitude), the deflection or curvature is great enough that the air starts spinning counterclockwise around the center of the storm.

storms.conditionsFinding: Penn State says at least five degrees from the equator; NASA Earth Observatory (2006) says generally at least 8. Penn State also notes the exception of Vamei, “formed at approximately 1.5 degrees North latitude near Singapore” (26 December 2001).

structure.q: Eye: The roughly circular area of comparatively light winds that encompasses the center of a severe tropical cyclone.
Eyewall / Wall Cloud: An organized band or ring of cumulonimbus clouds that surround the eye, or light-wind center of a tropical cyclone.
Surrounding the eye wall are curved bands of clouds that trail away in a spiral fashion, suitably called spiraling rain bands.
Storm Surge: An abnormal rise in sea level accompanying a hurricane or other intense storm

stages: Tropical disturbance
A discrete tropical weather system of apparently organized convection -- generally 100 to 300 nmi in diameter
Tropical depression
maximum sustained surface wind speed (using the U.S. 1-minute average) is 33 kt (38 mph or 62 km/hr) or less
Tropical storm
ranges from 34 kt (39 mph or 63 km/hr) to 63 kt (73 mph or 118 km/hr)
Hurricane
is 64 kt (74 mph or 119 km/hr) or more
Extratropical / post-tropical
a cyclone has lost its "tropical" characteristics

dissipation.q: These conditions include the storm moving over cooler water that can't supply warm, moist tropical air; the storm moving over land, again cutting off the source of warm, moist air; and finally, the storm moving into an area where strong winds high in the atmosphere disperse latent heat, reducing the warm temperatures aloft and raising the surface pressure.

season.q: Based on a 30-year climate period from 1991 to 2020, an average Atlantic hurricane season has 14 named storms, 7 hurricanes, and 3 major hurricanes (Category 3, 4, or 5 on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale).
season.q2: The peak of the Atlantic hurricane season is September 10, with most activity occurring between mid-August and mid-October.

history.name: Hurricane Katrina, 23–30 August 2005
history.q: Katrina was an extraordinarily powerful and deadly hurricane that carved a wide swath of catastrophic damage and inflicted large loss of life.
history.finding: Earlier versions of the report gave “over 1800 deaths”; the 2023 update gives 1392.
timeline: tropical depression over the southeastern Bahamas
145 kt — low-end Category 3 to Category 5 in under 12 h
extratropical low, absorbed in a front over the Great Lakes

history.name: Hurricane Andrew, 16–28 August 1992
history.q: Andrew was a small and ferocious Cape Verde hurricane that wrought unprecedented economic devastation along a path through the northwestern Bahamas, the southern Florida peninsula, and south-central Louisiana.
history.finding: The 2005 NHC addendum (after Landsea et al. 2004) raised the landfall intensity from 125 to 145 kt.

storms.name: Thunderstorm

intro.q: A thunderstorm is a rain shower during which you hear thunder. Since thunder comes from lightning, all thunderstorms have lightning.

conditions.q: Three basic ingredients are required for a thunderstorm to form: moisture, rising unstable air (air that keeps rising when given a nudge), and a lifting mechanism to provide the "nudge."

Severe supercell development is most likely in an environment possessing great buoyancy (CAPE) and large vertical wind shear. A Bulk Richardson Number of between 15 and 35 favor supercell development.

structure.q: An anvil forms when the updraft (warm air rising) has reached a point where the surrounding air is about the same temperature or even warmer. The cloud growth abruptly stops and flattens out to take the shape of an anvil.
A supercell is a long-lived (greater than 1 hour) and highly organized storm feeding off an updraft (a rising current of air) that is tilted and rotating.
A multi-cell storm is a common, garden-variety thunderstorm in which new updrafts form along the leading edge of rain-cooled air (the gust front).

stages: Developing
The developing stage of a thunderstorm is marked by a cumulus cloud that is being pushed upward by a rising column of air (updraft).
Mature
The thunderstorm enters the mature stage when the updraft continues to feed the storm, but precipitation begins to fall out of the storm, creating a downdraft (a column of air pushing downward).
Dissipating
Eventually, a large amount of precipitation is produced and the updraft is overcome by the downdraft beginning the dissipating stage.

dissipation.q: At the ground, the gust front moves out a long distance from the storm and cuts off the warm moist air that was feeding the thunderstorm.

season.q: Thunderstorms are most likely in the spring and summer months and during the afternoon and evening hours, but they can occur year-round and at all hours.
season.q2: Worldwide, there are an estimated 16 million thunderstorms each year, and at any given moment, there are roughly 2,000 thunderstorms in progress.

severe.q: A thunderstorm is classified as "severe" when it contains one or more of the following: hail one inch or greater, winds gusting in excess of 50 knots (57.5 mph), or a tornado.

storms.name: Tornado

intro.q: A tornado is a narrow, violently rotating column of air that extends from a thunderstorm to the ground.

conditions.q: One way a column of air can begin to rotate is from wind shear – when winds at two different levels above the ground blow at different speeds or in different directions.
The most destructive tornadoes occur from supercells, which are rotating thunderstorms with a well-defined radar circulation called a mesocyclone.

structure.q: A wall cloud is an isolated cloud lowering attached to the rain-free base of the thunderstorm.
There is no "eye" to a tornado like there is in a hurricane.

storms.stagesNote: No official stage-by-stage life cycle was found on the allowed NOAA pages; NSSL: “The truth is that we don't fully understand.”

dissipation.q: This time can range from an instant to several hours. The average is about five minutes.

season.q: The U.S. tornado threat shifts from the Southeast in the cooler months of the year, toward the southern and central Plains in May and June, and the northern Plains and Midwest during early summer.
season.q2: About 1,200 tornadoes hit the U.S. yearly.

history.name: Bridge Creek–Moore, Oklahoma, 3 May 1999 (tornado A9)
facts: 318 mph (Doppler on Wheels, near Bridge Creek)
history.q: The final total of 72 tornadoes makes May 3-4, 1999 event the largest outbreak of tornadoes for Oklahoma since official records began in 1950.
history.finding: NWS Norman: “Early results of this review process suggest that the maximum speed actually may be less than 318 mph (although it likely will remain above 300 mph).”

storms.name: Mid-latitude cyclone and fronts

intro.q: Extratropical Cyclone: A cyclone in the middle and high latitudes often being 2000 kilometers in diameter and usually containing a cold front that extends toward the equator for hundreds of kilometers.

conditions.q: a mid-latitude cyclone is born when an upper-level disturbance passes over a surface stationary front, creating a weak area of low pressure along it as divergence aloft reduces the weight of local air columns.

strong temperature gradients are required for mid-latitude cyclone development because the temperature advections play a key role in a positive feedback process that strengthens the cyclone (the cyclone strengthens itself).

structure.q: Cold Front: A zone separating two air masses, of which the cooler, denser mass is advancing and replacing the warmer.
Warm Front: A transition zone between a mass of warm air and the colder air it is replacing.
Occluded Front: A composite of two fronts, formed as a cold front overtakes a warm or quasi-stationary front.

stages: Birth on a stationary front
a mid-latitude cyclone is born when an upper-level disturbance passes over a surface stationary front
Warm and cold fronts, warm sector
East of the low, a warm front (which marks the retreat of colder air) develops … a cold front (which marks the leading edge of advancing cold air) forms west of the low
Occlusion
This separation occurs late in the cyclone's life, called "occlusion" (or "the occluded stage").
Decay
removed from strong surface temperature gradients and lacking upper-level divergence, the low weakens and dies

dissipation.q: So, removed from strong surface temperature gradients and lacking upper-level divergence, the low weakens and dies

season.q: (most mid-latitude cyclones last for a few days to a little more than a week)
season.q2: mid-latitude cyclones help the atmosphere strive for balance by reducing hemispheric temperature gradients.

history.name: Superstorm, 12–14 March 1993
facts: 43 in at Syracuse, NY; 56 in in Tennessee
history.q: Despite the strongly worded early warnings, the storm was responsible for some 200 deaths.
history.finding: NOAA’s 1994 assessment says “some 200” deaths; NWS Melbourne (2018) says 270 in 10 states.

storms.name: Blizzard and winter storm

intro.q: A winter storm is an event in which the main types of precipitation are snow, sleet or freezing rain.

conditions.q: Cold air. Below freezing temperatures in the clouds and near the ground are necessary to make snow and/or ice.
Lift. Something to raise the moist air to form the clouds and cause precipitation.
Moisture. To form clouds and precipitation.

structure.q: Precipitation continues to fall as snow when the temperature remains at or below 0 degrees Celsius from the cloud base to the ground.
snowflakes only partially melt when they fall through a shallow layer of warm air. These slushy drops refreeze as they next fall through a deep layer of freezing air above the surface

snowflakes descend into a warmer layer of air and melt completely. When these liquid water drops fall through another thin layer of freezing air just above the surface, they don't have enough time to refreeze before reaching the ground.

storms.stagesNote: Winter storms are usually mid-latitude cyclones — see that tab for the life cycle.

dissipation.q: Sometimes strong winds pick up snow that has already fallen, creating a ground blizzard.

season.q: Lake Effect Snow: Snow showers that are created when cold, dry air passes over a large warmer lake, such as one of the Great Lakes, and picks up moisture and heat.
season.q2: As a general rule, the threshold for potentially dangerous wind chill conditions is about -20°F and lower.

blizzard.q: A blizzard means that the following conditions are expected to prevail for a period of 3 hours or longer: Sustained wind or frequent gusts to 35 miles an hour or greater; and Considerable falling and/or blowing snow (i.e., reducing visibility frequently to less than ¼ mile)

storms.name: Heat wave

intro.q: Heat Wave: A period of abnormally and uncomfortably hot and unusually humid weather. Typically a heat wave lasts two or more days.

conditions.q: The principal cause of the July 1995 heat wave was a slow-moving, hot, and humid air mass produced by the chance occurrence at the same time of an unusually strong upper-level ridge of high pressure and unusually moist ground conditions.

structure.q: The Heat Index (HI) or the "Apparent Temperature" is an accurate measure of how hot it really feels when the Relative Humidity (RH) is added to the actual air temperature.

storms.stagesNote: No sourced stage sequence; heat waves end when the ridge of high pressure moves or breaks down (not quoted).

season.q: In a normal year, about 175 Americans succumb to the demands of summer heat.

history.name: Chicago and the Midwest, July 1995
history.q: Chicago experienced its worst weather-related disaster, with 465 heat-related deaths recorded during the period from July 11-27, 1995.
history.finding: Later non-report figures (739–750) were not verified; the NWS survey’s 465 is used.

intro.q: Monsoon: A thermally driven wind arising from differential heating between a land mass and the adjacent ocean that reverses its direction seasonally.

conditions.q: by late spring, strong solar heating causes temperatures to soar over these land areas. This intense heating causes surface air pressure to fall, forming an area of low pressure known as a thermal low.

Eventually, the pressure difference increases to the point that the cooler and more humid air over the ocean is drawn toward the hot, dry air over land. This moist air moving inland eventually becomes unstable and develops into thunderstorms.

structure.q: The outflow boundaries created by these strong thunderstorms can result in winds 50 mph or greater, and very dense blowing dust generated over open fields and desert.

dissipation.q: This cycle will continue until land areas begin to cool in the early fall, and water temperatures reach their peak in early fall. This reduces the pressure difference, which in turn causes the moist onshore flow to diminish and the monsoon gradually ends.

season.q: Our "monsoon season" officially extends from June 15th through September 30th
season.q2: For some areas, over 50% of annual rain falls during the monsoon.

sshws.q: The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale is a 1 to 5 rating based only on a hurricane's maximum sustained wind speed. This scale does not take into account other potentially deadly hazards such as storm surge, rainfall flooding, and tornadoes.
rows: Very dangerous winds will produce some damage
Extremely dangerous winds will cause extensive damage
sshws.oldFinding: NASA Earth Observatory’s 2006 page uses the pre-2012 ranges (e.g. Category 3 111–130 mph); the NHC table is used.

ef.q: The EF scale still is a set of wind estimates (not measurements) based on damage.
ef.since: The Enhanced Fujita Scale or EF Scale, which became operational on February 1, 2007, is used to assign a tornado a 'rating' based on estimated wind speeds and related damage.

heatIndex.valid: The Rothfusz regression is not valid for extreme temperature and relative humidity conditions beyond the range of data considered by Steadman.
